ding-ding-zyun.title: Round and Round, the Chrysanthemum Garden
ding-ding-zyun.subtitle: A nursery rhyme you sing in a circle
ding-ding-zyun.quote: Round and round, the chrysanthemum garden.
ding-ding-zyun.intro: On the park grass, the children stand in a circle. They sing as they turn. Grandma waves to you: do you want to join the circle?

ding-1.title: A Circle on the Grass
ding-1.text: School is out, and the park grass is busy. Grandma holds your hand and points ahead: “Look, the big kids are in a circle. They are singing the round-and-round rhyme. Do you want to go in?”

ding-2a.title: Round and Round, Chrysanthemum Garden
ding-2a.text: You step into the circle and hold the hand next to you. Everyone sings as they turn: “Round and round, chrysanthemum garden, puffed-rice cakes, sticky rice balls.” By the third turn, your head feels a little dizzy.

ding-2b.title: The Little One Outside the Circle
ding-2b.text: You sit on a bench and watch. A child smaller than you stands outside the circle. One finger is in their mouth. They want to go in, but they are afraid.

ding-3a.title: Ending · No One Left Out
ding-3a.text: You slow your steps and hold the hand beside you tight. The circle turns more and more smoothly. Laughter spreads, ring after ring. Grandma claps beside you: “That's right. When we make a circle, no one is left behind.”
ding-3a.endingText: In a circle, no one is left out.

ding-3b.title: Ending · A Circle Has No Ends
ding-3b.text: You sit with Grandma in the shade of a tree and watch the circle on the grass. Grandma says: “A circle has no start and no end. You can step in any time. Next time, you can be the first one to reach out a hand.”
ding-3b.endingText: A circle has no ends. You can join any time.

ding-1: Walk into the circle and join in
Stand beside it and watch for a while
ding-2a: Keep the beat and turn slowly
ding-2b: Take their hand and bring them into the circle
Ask Grandma why people make a circle

氹氹转.note: In Cantonese rhymes it describes children turning in a circle.

围圈.note: Everyone holds hands and makes a circle.

炒米饼.meaning: a small cake made of puffed rice
炒米饼.note: A Cantonese treat often made for the New Year.

糯米圆.meaning: little balls made of sticky rice

细过.note: In Cantonese, “sai” means young or small.

唔敢.note: Wanting to try, but a little scared.

漏低.note: In Cantonese it means leaving a person or thing behind.

拍手.note: People clap when they are happy.

树荫.meaning: the cool shade under a tree
树荫.note: A favourite spot to rest on a hot summer day.

几时.note: Cantonese often uses “gei si” to ask about time.

dim-cung-cung.title: Tap, Tap, Little Bug
dim-cung-cung.subtitle: A little bug on your fingertip
dim-cung-cung.quote: Tap, tap, little bug. Little bug, fly.
dim-cung-cung.intro: Mum taps your palm softly with her finger and sings “Tap, tap, little bug. Little bug, fly.” Then a real little bug flies over.

dim-1.title: A Little Bug on Your Palm
dim-1.text: The courtyard is quiet. Mum sits beside you and taps your palm with her finger: “Tap, tap, little bug. Little bug, fly, fly to the lychee garden.” Just then, a small red-and-black bug flies past.

dim-2a.title: The Bug Lands on a Lychee Leaf
dim-2a.text: The little bug flies on and on, then lands on a lychee leaf. You stand on tiptoe and walk over slowly. Its wings are thin and thin, and they shine a little in the sun.

dim-2b.title: Two Fingers Make a Little Bug
dim-2b.text: Mum shows you how to hold up two fingers and open and close them: “Tap, tap, little bug. Little bug, fly.” You try a few times, and your fingers move more and more smoothly.

dim-3a.title: Ending · Wave Goodbye
dim-3a.text: The little bug flaps its wings and flies over the wall. You wave: “Come and play another day.” Mum smiles: “The little bug has to go home for dinner. Let's go and wash our hands too.”
dim-3a.endingText: Watching is enough. You don't have to catch it.

dim-3b.title: Ending · Bugs Have Wings, You Have Fingers
dim-3b.text: You reach out to catch it, but the little bug has already flown high. Mum laughs: “The bug has wings. You have two fingers. Come on, let's play the tapping game again.”
dim-3b.endingText: The little bug has wings. You have two fingers.

dim-1: Stay and learn the finger game
dim-2b: Ask where the little bug is going

点虫虫.meaning: to tap with a finger, a game played with small children
点虫虫.note: You tap the palm and sing the rhyme.

荔枝基.meaning: a lychee orchard, or the ground under lychee trees
荔枝基.note: Lychee orchards are common in the Pearl River Delta.

跷高脚.note: You walk lightly so you do not scare the bug.

薄薄哋.note: The ending “dei” means a little, or a bit.

郁.note: In Cantonese, “juk” means to move or wiggle.

手指公.note: Each of the five fingers has its own name.

振翅.note: Birds and bugs flap their wings before they fly.

第日.note: In Cantonese it means a day in the future.

扑.note: You can “pok” at a butterfly or a bug.

翼.note: Cantonese speakers often say “jik” in everyday talk.

pai-pai-sit-fan-gwo.title: Sit in a Row and Eat Fan Guo
pai-pai-sit-fan-gwo.subtitle: One basket of fan guo, a share for everyone
pai-pai-sit-fan-gwo.quote: Sit in a row, eat fan guo.
pai-pai-sit-fan-gwo.intro: Grandma has just steamed a basket of fan guo. Steam curls up into the air. Five children gather round. How can everyone get some?

pai-1.title: One Hot Basket of Fan Guo
pai-1.text: Grandma lifts the steamer lid. White steam rises. The fan guo in the basket look clear and shiny. Five children stand around the table. You count: one, two, three… twelve in all.

pai-2a.title: While We Queue
pai-2a.text: You stand at the end of the line. The child in front of you takes three fan guo at once. The children behind start to shout: “Then what about us?”

pai-2b.title: Sharing to the Last One
pai-2b.text: You help Grandma share them out, one by one. When you reach the last child, only one fan guo is left in the basket. But two people still have none. You look at the one in your own hand.

pai-3a.title: Ending · A Share for Everyone
pai-3a.text: Everyone sits down. Two each, just right. Grandma gives you one more: “You know how to sit in a row, so everyone gets a share.” The fan guo are piping hot. You take a bite, and the filling runs out.
pai-3a.endingText: Sit in a row, eat fan guo, and everyone gets a share.

pai-3b.title: Ending · Steam One More Basket
pai-3b.text: Grandma says: “If that's not enough, we'll steam one more basket.” You all sit in a row and wait for the steam to rise again. Grandma says: “Fan guo must be steamed through. You can't rush it. Wait a little, and everyone will get some.”
pai-3b.endingText: Wait a little. Hot and fresh tastes best.

pai-1: Line up and take one at a time
pai-2a: Let it go and take fewer yourself
pai-2b: Give yours to the smallest child

粉果.meaning: a Cantonese steamed dumpling with a see-through wrapper and filling inside
粉果.note: A common dim sum in old tea houses.

蒸笼.note: Baskets are stacked up to steam the food.

队尾.note: In a line, one person follows another.

嘈.note: In Cantonese, “cou” means a loud, busy noise.

分.note: You give things out piece by piece.

仲有.note: In Cantonese, “zung” means still or more.

啱啱好.note: Not too much, not too little.

热辣辣.note: It describes food straight from the pot or steamer.

一阵.note: In Cantonese it means a very short time.

lok-jyu-daai.title: Heavy Rain, Flooded Street
lok-jyu-daai.subtitle: A big rainstorm under the arcade
lok-jyu-daai.intro: You are halfway out on an errand when the sky suddenly turns dark. The rain comes down hard. The arcade is full of people. How will you get home?

rain-1.title: The Rain Comes Down Hard
rain-1.text: You and Mum go out to buy food. Halfway there, the sky turns dark all at once. Raindrops as big as beans come down, and the water soon covers your feet. Mum holds you back: “Don't panic. There is an arcade up ahead.”

rain-2a.title: Puddles and Baskets of Greens
rain-2a.text: You run out into the rain and hop over puddles one by one. At the corner, an old lady carries two baskets of greens on a pole. She walks very slowly, and her umbrella is tilting.

rain-2b.title: A Wait Under the Arcade
rain-2b.text: You stand under the arcade. Rain runs down from the tiles along the eaves, like a curtain of water. Nearby, a child wants to step into a deep puddle. Even their shoes are wet.

rain-3a.title: Ending · A Rainbow After the Rain
rain-3a.text: You carry one basket of greens for the old lady, and she walks you to your building. The rain slowly grows lighter, and a rainbow appears in the sky. She says: “Heavy rain is nothing to fear. Just walk slowly.”
rain-3a.endingText: Heavy rain, flooded street — walk slowly and you'll be fine.

rain-3b.title: Ending · Wait, and the Rain Will Stop
rain-3b.text: You sit under the arcade and count the raindrops: one, two, three… By the time you reach a hundred, the rain really is softer. Mum comes to meet you: “The puddles are deep. Don't step in them. Wait a little, and the rain will stop.”
rain-3b.endingText: Wait a little. The rain will stop, and the sky will clear.

rain-1: Wait under the arcade until the rain stops
rain-2b: Tell them not to step into the deep water

落雨大.note: In Cantonese, “lok jyu” means rain falls.

骑楼.meaning: a covered walkway on the ground floor of a building
骑楼.note: A common Xiguan building style, handy for sheltering from rain.

水氹.note: The water that gathers on the ground after rain.

担.meaning: to carry on a shoulder pole
担.note: You use your shoulder to carry the load.

瓦檐.meaning: the edge of a tiled roof
瓦檐.note: Rain drips down from the eaves.

水帘.note: It describes rain pouring down from the eaves.

天虹.note: Cantonese also calls it “hung”. You often see one after rain.

细.note: “Jyu sai zo” means the rain has grown lighter.

雨点.note: Rain falling one drop at a time.

真系.note: Cantonese often uses “zan hai” to mean truly.

nin-jaa-baat-sai-laat-taai.title: The Twenty-Eighth: Scrub the Old Year Clean
nin-jaa-baat-sai-laat-taai.subtitle: Washing the old year away to welcome the new one
nin-jaa-baat-sai-laat-taai.quote: On the twenty-eighth, wash the dirt away.
nin-jaa-baat-sai-laat-taai.intro: On the twenty-eighth day of the last lunar month, the whole family cleans the house. Mum gives you the windows. Grandma asks you to sort out old things. Do old things always have to be thrown away?

nin-1.title: The Twenty-Eighth: Big Clean-Up
nin-1.text: It is the twenty-eighth day of the last lunar month, and the house is a mess. Mum washes the bedding. Dad wipes the fan. Grandma hands you a cloth: “You do the windows. When you finish, tidy your own desk.” You look at everything in the flat and don't know where to start.

nin-2a.title: Window Paper-Cuts and Old Couplets
nin-2a.text: You wipe along the window. Last year's paper-cuts have faded, and their corners have curled up. Grandma says: “Tear the old ones off and put up new ones. A new year, a fresh start.” You are still holding a paper-cut you made when you were little.

nin-2b.title: Old Things Under the Desk
nin-2b.text: You tidy under the desk and find a wooden horse you played with as a toddler, a stack of red envelope packets, and a photo of you with Grandpa. Mum says: “If it's no use, throw it out. Don't stuff it all back.” You look at the wooden horse. You can't bear to part with it.

nin-3a.title: Ending · A New Year, a Fresh Start
nin-3a.text: The windows shine. The new couplets are pasted up straight and neat. Grandma ties up all the rubbish in the house: “Wash away the old year and welcome the new one. When the house is clean, people feel brighter too.” You look at the shining window and smile.
nin-3a.endingText: Wash the dirt away. Wash off the old year. Welcome the new one.

nin-3b.title: Ending · Keep the Old Story
nin-3b.text: You find a tin box and put the wooden horse, the red envelopes and the photo inside. You stick on a label: “My Old Year.” Grandma watches you and smiles: “Old things don't take up much room. Keeping the story is enough.”
nin-3b.endingText: Old things can stay. So can their stories.

nin-2a: Put up the new spring couplets
nin-2b: Give the wooden horse to your cousin
Make a memory box and keep it

年廿八.meaning: the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth lunar month
年廿八.note: In Cantonese custom, this is the day for the big clean.

洗邋遢.meaning: to clean the house from top to bottom
洗邋遢.note: It means washing away the old year's bad luck.

窗花.note: People put them up for New Year, in lucky red.

挥春.meaning: red paper couplets or lucky words pasted up at Spring Festival

利是封.note: Used for lucky money at New Year.

唔舍得.meaning: can't bear to part with it
唔舍得.note: You have feelings for old things.

正正.note: Couplets should be pasted up straight.

铁盒.note: In the old days, people kept biscuits and photos in tin boxes.

阻地方.note: In Cantonese, “zo” means to block or take up room.
